title: Arafah and Ashura
hook: two voluntary fasts that expiate sins of past years (Muslim)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fast of Dawud, and your line: a day on, a day off. Did you give something a day of rest? Day one thousand one hundred fourteen.

Someone once asked the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ about fasting on two particular days of the year. His answers are kept in Sahih Muslim, and they reach a long way. Fasting one of them, he said, wipes away the sins of the year before and the year after. Fasting the other wipes away the sins of the year before. Two single days, each reaching across a whole year or more. Neither is required. Both are remembered. One sits near the start of the Islamic year, the other near its end. Today, Arafah and Ashura.
screen: `A QUESTION ABOUT TWO DAYS.` → `ONE DAY, TWO YEARS.` → `NEAR THE START, NEAR THE END.`

segments.voice: First, Arafah. It's the ninth day of Dhul Hijjah, the month of pilgrimage, the day the pilgrims stand on the plain of Arafah near Mecca, in prayer until sunset. Muslims who aren't on the pilgrimage can join that day from home by fasting it. That's the fast the hadith in Muslim ties to the year before and the year after. Second, a surprise: the pilgrims themselves are not fasting. In Sahih al-Bukhari, people at Arafah weren't sure whether the Prophet was fasting that day. Umm al-Fadl sent him a cup of milk, and he drank it, in front of everyone, while standing there. The standing is the work of that day for the pilgrim; the fast belongs to those at home. Third, Ashura, the tenth of Muharram, the first month. A report in Bukhari says that when the Prophet came to Medina, he found the Jews of the city fasting that day, and they told him it was the day God saved Musa, Moses, and his people. He fasted it and told the Muslims to fast it. A report in Muslim adds that late in his life he said, if he lived to the next year, he would fast the ninth as well. So some Sunni Muslims fast the ninth and tenth together. Fourth, Ashura carries another weight. Tradition remembers it as the day of Karbala, where Husayn, the Prophet's grandson, was killed with his family and companions. Shia communities keep Ashura above all as a day of mourning for Husayn, with gatherings, recitations and grief, and Shia scholars have their own rulings on fasting it. The same day, held two ways, each with its reasons. Put together: one day on a plain where pilgrims stand, and one day that remembers both a people saved and a grandson lost.
screen: `ARAFAH: THE NINTH OF DHUL HIJJAH.` · `THE PILGRIM DRINKS THE MILK.` · `ASHURA: THE DAY MUSA WAS SAVED.` · `KARBALA, AND A DAY OF MOURNING.`

segments.voice: The practice: plan one of them. Settle, and let your shoulders drop. Arafah comes in the month of pilgrimage; Ashura in the first month of the year. You don't need the dates right now. Choose one of the two days in your mind. If you're Muslim and you fast, picture the morning of that fast: what you'd eat before dawn, who you'd tell. If not, picture what you might do on that day to remember what it holds, a pilgrim's standing, or a family's grief. Hold the picture. The bell holds the time.
Arafah and Ashura. The ninth of Dhul Hijjah and the tenth of Muharram, two voluntary fasts, each tied in Sahih Muslim to the wiping away of a year's sins. Today's word.
Your line: two special fasts. Today, find out when the next of the two falls, and write it down somewhere you'll see it. Tomorrow: the odd nights. Day one thousand one hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: Some Sunni Muslims fast the day of Arafah when not on pilgrimage, and fast Ashura with the day before it; for Shia Muslims, Ashura is a day of mourning for Husayn, marked with gatherings, and their scholars give their own rulings on fasting.

notes: Muslim 1162 (Arafah expiates the year before and after; Ashura the year before): confirm number.
Bukhari 1988 (Umm al-Fadl's cup of milk at Arafah): confirm number.
Bukhari 2004 (Jews of Medina fasting Ashura, the day Musa was saved): confirm number. The line 'we have more right to Musa than you' was deliberately left out to avoid any appearance of ranking.
Muslim 1134 (fasting the ninth as well): confirm number.
'some Sunni Muslims fast the ninth and tenth together' is general practice, not in the cited texts; confirm.
Shia practice on Ashura (mourning for Husayn; rulings on fasting) is summarized deliberately briefly; a Shia Keeper should check the wording.
'praying from midday until sunset' at Arafah: confirm phrasing.
